newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu delays Sharon appointment.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu delays Sharon appointment.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delayed on Wednesday a shakeup of his fractious cabinet that could give the hawkish Ariel Sharon more power and sound alarm bells across the Middle East.

The former general, an architect of Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon and a champion of Jewish settlement in the West Bank and Gaza, was poised to be named finance minister and has demanded to be included in an inner team of top decision makers.

Analysts said Foreign Minister David Levy, a coalition ally who withheld his support from Netanyahu in a parliamentary no-confidence vote on Tuesday which the prime minister survived, opposed giving Sharon a stronger hand in policy-making.

"I am certain we all appreciate the wide experience of minister Sharon and his great knowledge," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said. "If the prime minister decides to include him in this team it will certainly be for the good of Israel."
But Bazak told Israel Radio the reshuffle, which the Likud party leader had hoped to present to parliament this week, would be delayed.
"I imagine it will be finished in the coming days," he said.

Sharon is currently national infrastructure minister but not in a "kitchen cabinet" of insiders who hammer out strategy in a Middle East peace process, now in deep crisis over the building of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Israeli media reports said Levy, a relative moderate in Netanyahu's rightist-religious government, had threatened to resign if Sharon got into the inner policy team. Levy maintained public silence.
For Arabs, the name Sharon brings up bitter memories of the 1982 massacre by Christian militiamen of Palestinians in two Beirut refugee camps surrounded by the Israeli army.

An Israeli inquiry found Sharon indirectly responsible, forcing him to quit as defence chief in 1983. But he bounded back in other cabinet posts and ploughed the way for settlement expansion, angering Israel's main ally, the United States.
The reshuffle delay was another embarrassment for Netanyahu, who has lurched from crisis to crisis in a year in office.

He won Tuesday's parliamentary vote 55-50 -- no-confidence motions need to win the support of at least 61 legislators in the 120-seat Knesset to pass -- but 11 of 66 coalition members pointedly did not back him.
Disgruntled coalition partners complain of mismanagement by Netanyahu, whose ill-fated appointment of an attorney-general earlier this year nearly got him indicted.

"The negative conclusion is that the prime minister cannot trust Gesher or the rebels in the Likud," political analyst Hanan Crystal said. "He must calm and compensate and bring David Levy closer again. That is the key."

Funding for various social welfare projects could do the trick. Levy's Gesher, which counts on Jews of North African or Middle Eastern descent for the bulk of its support, has pledged to improve the economic standing of low-income Israelis.

But in the long run, Netanyahu faced a Likud leadership challenge from Dan Meridor, the finance minister who quit last week in a dispute over foreign exchange policy that masked a years-long rivalry between the two men.

"I don't think it would be right that in the next elections Israelis will have to decide between a Labour party candidate...and Mr Netanyahu. I want to fight so that that will not be the choice," Meridor told Israel Radio.
Ehud Barak, leader of the main opposition Labour party, said the no-confidence vote was "the beginning of the countdown to returning Israel to responsible hands".

In a rancorous speech in parliament on Tuesday, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi set the stage for what is likely to be a key Likud striking point against Barak in the next elections -- scheduled for the year 2000.

He said the former army chief "fled" the scene of a 1992 training accident, abandoning wounded soldiers. Barak, Israel's most decorated soldier, has denied the allegation, saying he left the scene in a helicopter only after making sure they were receiving medical attention.
